A1-A2.headline: The History of the Medieval Balkan Slave Trade

pages.text: Have you ever wondered how people were traded in the Middle Ages? Between the 7th and 15th centuries, a slave trade existed in the Balkan region. Traders took captives across the sea to sell them in other lands.
pages.caption: Slavic populations living in the medieval Balkan region.

evidence.articleCaption: Illustration of Sclaveni between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains

pages.text: Religion was very important during the Middle Ages. People of one religion were not allowed to enslave others who shared their faith. However, people from different religions were seen as valid targets. The Balkans was a border zone between different religious groups.

Slaves captured in the Balkans were sent to two main places. Some were taken to Southern Europe to work as domestic servants in Italy and Spain. Others were shipped in larger numbers to the Islamic Middle East.

In Egypt, many young male slaves were trained to become soldier guards known as Mamluks. This trade continued for hundreds of years until the Ottoman Empire conquered the region and changed the trade routes forever.

B1-B2.headline: Venice and the Medieval Balkan Slave Trade Network

pages.text: What drove the movement of thousands of people across the medieval Adriatic Sea? The Balkan slave trade was a major economic network from the 7th to the mid-15th century. Venetian merchants transported captives from the Balkans to markets in Southern Europe and the Middle East.
pages.caption: Illustration depicting Slavic groups in the Balkan region.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Први Словени између Дунава и Балкана.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Illustration of Sclaveni between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains

pages.text: This trade flourished because the Balkans served as a religious border zone. Medieval customs strictly prohibited the enslavement of fellow believers, but populations of different faiths were deemed legitimate targets. Consequently, pagan, Orthodox Christian, and Bogomil communities became primary sources for merchants.

Bosnians adhering to Bogomilism were especially targeted since their faith was not acknowledged as mainstream Christianity. The profits generated from this extensive trafficking played a crucial role in establishing the Republic of Venice as a prosperous maritime trading empire.

While women were often sold as domestic servants in Italy and Spain, thousands of young boys were shipped annually to the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt. These youths were trained as elite military slaves known as Mamluks, sustaining military power until the Ottoman conquest reshaped the region.

C1-C2.headline: Geopolitics and Religious Frontiers in the Balkan Slave Trade

pages.text: Spanning from the early Middle Ages through the mid-fifteenth century, the Balkan slave trade functioned as a vital commercial conduit. Venetian merchants systematically trafficked individuals from the Balkan interior across the Adriatic and Aegean basins toward Southern European markets and the Islamic Middle East.
pages.caption: Depiction of Sclaveni populations.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Први Словени између Дунава и Балкана.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Illustration of Sclaveni between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains

pages.text: The structural foundation of this commerce rested upon medieval theological boundaries. Because religious doctrine forbade the subjugation of co-religionists while condoning the enslavement of outsiders and heretics, the politically decentralized and unstable Balkan peninsula emerged as an optimal supply reservoir.

Bosnian adherents of Bogomilism experienced severe targeting due to their rejection by mainstream Christian authorities. Interestingly, legal circumventions also occurred; Albanian children were sometimes categorized as contract workers rather than slaves to technically bypass religious prohibitions against enslaving fellow Christians.

While European destinations absorbed domestic maid servants, the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt imported thousands of young males annually to replenish its military caste. Ultimately, fifteenth-century Ottoman expansion dissolved this autonomous trade network, laying structural preconditions that later influenced transatlantic commerce.
